name: Capy

modes.label: Per-thread VM, billed hourly by size while awake
modes.note: Coding-agent VM (one per thread): a Firecracker microVM with its own Linux 6.1 kernel, Ubuntu 24.04, hosted on Latitude.sh bare metal in the United States since 2026-10-15 (was Daytona; capy.ai/subprocessors). Billed per hour by size only while awake (+2 min wind-down); sleeps ~2 min after the thread stops, unless a background command (up to 6 h), an open shell/desktop/preview tab, preview traffic (5 min per request, up to 4 h after the last thread use) or the manual 'Keep awake 4h' holds it; asleep = free, disk kept, deleted after 30 days asleep. Size is set per project. Model tokens billed separately from the same credit balance. Size table (docs.capy.ai/machines#specs, verified 2026-11-08): Small 1/4/64 $0.10, Medium 2/8/64 $0.20, Large 4/16/64 $0.40 (default), Ultra 8/32/64 $0.80, Hyper 16/64/128 $1.60 per hour; Big Guy 16/128/256 $3.20 is 'On request' (not priced here). boot_overhead_s 120 = the 2-minute billed wind-down per awake period. Billing granularity not stated. Plans cap machine size and total concurrent RAM (capy.ai/pricing, checked 2026-10-14): Lite 4 CPU / 16 GB machines, 128 GB at once; Pro 8 CPU / 32 GB, 512 GB; Max 16 CPU / 64 GB, 1 TB.

plans.name: Lite monthly
plans.note: Pricing page (checked 2026-10-14): "128 GB concurrent RAM on cloud machines" / "Cloud machines up to 4 CPU / 16 GB" (Small, Medium, Large only).

plans.name: Pro monthly
plans.note: Pricing page (checked 2026-10-14): "512 GB concurrent RAM on cloud machines" / "Cloud machines up to 8 CPU / 32 GB" (up to Ultra).

plans.name: Max base monthly
plans.note: Pricing page (checked 2026-10-14): "1 TB concurrent RAM on cloud machines" / "Cloud machines up to 16 CPU / 64 GB" (Hyper is Max-only). 1 TB taken as 1024 GiB.

plans.name: Pay-as-you-go balance (no plan)
plans.note: An organization can run entirely on purchased balance; min top-up $5 at 1:1. Machine capacity without a plan is not published ("Plans set your monthly credits and how much cloud machine capacity you can run"), so this row likely has a cap at or below Lite (128 GB concurrent RAM, 4 CPU / 16 GB machines) that the card cannot state.

caveats: Lite $20/mo includes $20 credits, Pro $100 includes $105, Max $200–1000 in $100 steps includes 110%; annual 20% discount, trial $1/7d/card. Credits pay agent/model work and resource exchange unverified; unlimited members not unlimited compute.
Null values mean unknown, not free/unlimited. No model-token cost, tax or unverified ancillary charge included.
Native browser/device/task/credit prices with unknown CPU/RAM are deliberately non-priceable. Check regime before interpreting any partial resource estimate.
Programs: approved OSS orgs get $50 free usage per UTC day; YC companies and eligible Solo Founders members get $1,000 credits (program-gated).
Drive (formerly Volumes; org/project files outside git): "1 GB on Free, 10 GB on Lite, 25 GB on Pro, and 50 GB on Max"; 100 MiB per file, 2 GiB per saved version; no overage price published.

No always-on mode: a machine sleeps about 2 minutes after the thread stops, unless a background command (up to 6 h), an open shell/desktop/preview tab, preview traffic (5 min per request, up to 4 h after the last thread use) or the manual 'Keep awake 4h' holds it. "A process the agent leaves running, such as a dev server, doesn't hold the machine awake" (docs.capy.ai/machines).

No /dev/kvm, so no accelerated emulators or nested VMs inside the machine. Pro, Max and Enterprise can attach real iOS and Android cloud phones (via Revyl) to a thread: $5.40/h for iPhone or iPad, $3.60/h for Android, billed in credits while awake (docs.capy.ai/cloud-phones).

Agents: Capy runs its own agent, or Claude Code mode (Claude Agent SDK) when you connect a Claude Pro/Max plan. Codex, Copilot and SuperGrok subscriptions supply models to Capy's agent. No documented way to run another harness (docs.capy.ai/models-and-pricing).
Threads can also run on your own computer through the Capy desktop app and move to the cloud and back (docs.capy.ai/welcome).
OIDC federation gives machines short-lived Google Cloud, AWS, Azure or Vault tokens, with no stored keys (docs.capy.ai/cloud-credentials).

fleet.verification: $1 seven-day Lite intro requires a verified card, limited to one intro per card and organization.
fleet.tiers: Lite/Pro/Max advertise unlimited concurrent threads but cap concurrent machine RAM: Lite 128 GB (machines up to 4 CPU / 16 GB), Pro 512 GB (up to 8 CPU / 32 GB), Max 1 TB (up to 16 CPU / 64 GB); Enterprise custom terms.
fleet.notes: Thread count is unlimited but running machines are capped by plan concurrent RAM ("Plans set your monthly credits and how much cloud machine capacity you can run"). Capacity without a plan, Enterprise limits, CPU/GPU quotas and review times remain unknown.

audit_2026_09_29.source: checked against the provider's live pricing and docs pages

snapshot_auto.quote: The filesystem survives sleep. Memory, processes, and network connections do not. Resume is a cold boot from disk: your checkout and installed packages are intact, but every process is gone.
snapshot_auto.note: Machines auto-sleep ~2 min after the thread stops working and cold-boot from the persisted disk on wake (persistent_disk, not a state snapshot). A machine asleep for 30 days is deleted ('A machine that sleeps for 30 days is deleted.').

snapshot_on_demand.quote: A snapshot is your project's post-setup filesystem (repositories cloned, dependencies installed, `initialize` already run) baked into a bootable image. ... Trigger a build immediately from the same page, or ask Capy to build one now.
snapshot_on_demand.note: Only project setup-image snapshots: built by re-running the setup recipe on a dedicated build machine (hourly or on demand), disk only, used to boot new machines in ~1-2 s. No documented way to snapshot/checkpoint a specific running machine's state or fork it.

harness_api.quote: The Capy API gives programmatic access to the same platform the app uses: create threads, send messages, watch the agent work, and read what it produced. ... A **thread** is a durable agent conversation on Capy's servers, with a VM attached for execution.
harness_api.note: Harness = Capy's own agent (Captain + subagents, formerly called tasks) only, with many models (Claude/GPT/Gemini/Grok/Kimi/GLM/Qwen). REST: create thread with prompt, send/interrupt messages, read transcript, list threads, observe subagent tree (read-only), and Server-Sent Events streams on a thread or subagent (docs.capy.ai/api-reference/overview: "Hold a Server-Sent Events connection on a thread or subagent"). Caveat: the agent loop runs on Capy's servers, not inside the VM ('The agent loop runs on Capy's servers; the machine is where execution happens'). With a connected Claude Pro/Max plan, threads run in Claude Code mode (Claude Agent SDK) through the same API; Codex CLI is not run.

guest_firewall.note: Each thread gets its own Firecracker microVM (own Linux 6.1 kernel, Ubuntu 24.04) with passwordless sudo, and Docker Engine (which itself programs iptables) runs inside.

secret_proxy.quote: Capy encrypts them at rest, injects them into the machine's process environment at boot ... the machine is the agent's execution environment, so code the agent runs can read anything on the machine, including your variables.
secret_proxy.note: User secrets are env vars on the machine. BUT a narrow first-party credential-injecting proxy exists for GitHub/git only: 'Every git operation routes through Capy's proxy, which injects credentials server-side; the machine holds only a bearer scoped to itself' (docs.capy.ai/secrets, /admin/security). Model-provider keys are never on the machine because the agent loop runs server-side. Not configurable for arbitrary hosts. Separately, OIDC federation lets machines sign in to Google Cloud, AWS, Azure, Vault or any OIDC service 'with short-lived tokens Capy signs, with no stored keys' (docs.capy.ai/cloud-credentials).

volume_attach.quote: Capy Drive stores instructions, skills, and files outside git so every thread in a scope can use them.
volume_attach.note: Capy Drive (formerly Volumes) is a versioned file store (AGENTS.md, skills, saved files) the agent saves to, not attachable block/network volumes. Disk tier is fixed by machine size (64/128/256 GB).

volume_shared.quote: Each task can run on its own machine, and machines don't share a filesystem. Capy copies files and directories between machines with its `transfer_files` tool, the only cross-machine path.
volume_shared.note: Org/project Drive files are shared across threads as saved files (versioned), not a live concurrently mounted FS.

isolation.quote: Firecracker microVM with its own Linux 6.1 kernel, isolated from every other machine
isolation.note: Hosted on Latitude.sh bare metal in the United States: 'Latitude.sh replaces Daytona as the host for agent cloud machines' (capy.ai/subprocessors changelog, 2026-10-15).

image_oci.quote: The environment is your project's machine recipe: which setup scripts prepare a fresh machine ... A snapshot is your project's post-setup filesystem ... baked into a bootable image.
image_oci.note: Machines always boot from a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 image or a Capy-built snapshot produced by running your setup scripts; there is no documented way to supply your own Docker/OCI image.

nested_virt.quote: There is no `/dev/kvm`, so the accelerated Android emulator, QEMU with KVM, Firecracker, and VirtualBox don't work or fall back to slow software emulation.
nested_virt.note: Docker runs inside the machine. For mobile testing, Pro and above attach real iOS/Android cloud phones via Revyl ($5.40/h iPhone or iPad, $3.60/h Android; docs.capy.ai/cloud-phones), which is a separate device, not nested virtualization.

computer_use.quote: The thread pane shows the machine as the agent uses it: terminal output for commands, the growing diff, a file browser, and a live desktop view of the machine's display, useful when the agent is driving a browser or you asked it to open your app. You never need SSH to see what's happening.
computer_use.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — the live desktop view is for watching Capy's own coding agent drive its browser; there is no user-facing API to drive the desktop by screenshots/clicks.

anti_bot.quote: Capy is the best AI software engineer. Delegate tasks to parallel coding agents that plan, build, and ship — from task to merged PR.
anti_bot.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — Capy is a background coding-agent platform, not a browser-automation/scraping product; no anti-bot/stealth feature is documented.

captcha_solving.quote: Capy is the best AI software engineer. Delegate tasks to parallel coding agents that plan, build, and ship — from task to merged PR.
captcha_solving.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — no CAPTCHA-solving feature is documented for this coding-agent platform.

egress_ip_type.quote: Teams using Capy often ask us if we have static outbound IPs they can allow-list ... Since every Capy thread runs in its own isolated sandbox machine with dynamic addresses, it's hard for us to provide a static list of IP addresses.
egress_ip_type.note: Machines run on Latitude.sh bare metal in the United States (capy.ai/subprocessors, since 2026-10-15) with dynamic, non-static outbound addresses: datacenter egress, not residential/mobile.

ssh.quote: There is no SSH. Open a shell or the machine's desktop from the + menu in the thread pane.
ssh.note: An interactive shell, desktop and file browser are in the app. Threads can also run on your own computer through the desktop app (docs.capy.ai/welcome).

fork.quote: A snapshot is your project's post-setup filesystem (repositories cloned, dependencies installed, initialize already run) baked into a bootable image. A fresh machine that restores from one skips the clone and setup work entirely.
fork.note: not offered: snapshots exist only to speed up booting a fresh machine from a cached setup image; there is no documented feature to clone/fork an existing machine into new independent copies.

fork_running.quote: The filesystem survives sleep. Memory, processes, and network connections do not. Resume is a cold boot from disk: your checkout and installed packages are intact, but every process is gone.
fork_running.note: not offered: no clone-a-running-machine capability is documented; even the machine's own resume path is a cold boot, not a live clone.

memory_snapshot_fork.quote: The filesystem survives sleep. Memory, processes, and network connections do not. Resume is a cold boot from disk.
memory_snapshot_fork.note: not offered: snapshots/resume are disk-only; memory and running processes are never preserved or forked.

wake_on_request.quote: When the machine is asleep, the URL shows a Start the machine link that asks you to sign in and wakes it.
wake_on_request.note: An anonymous request does not wake a sleeping machine; a signed-in user clicks a link to wake it. While awake, 'Each request to the preview keeps the machine awake 5 more minutes, for up to 4 hours after you or the agent last used the thread.'

live_resize.quote: Large is the default and handles most work. Go bigger for heavy builds and large test suites; a size change applies to new machines, not ones already running.
live_resize.note: Explicitly stated: resizing only affects newly created machines, not a running one.

agent_harnesses.quote: A Claude Pro or Max plan runs Claude models in Claude Code mode. ... it runs on the Claude Agent SDK, and Capy's tools, machines, subagents, and pull requests work the same inside it.
agent_harnesses.how: connect a Claude Pro or Max plan (paste a `claude setup-token` token) to run threads in Claude Code mode
agent_harnesses.note: Claude Code (Agent SDK) is the one third-party harness. Codex, Copilot and SuperGrok subscriptions only supply models to Capy's own agent. No documented way to run another harness such as Codex CLI or OpenCode.

own_agent_api.quote: The Capy API gives programmatic access to the same platform the app uses: create threads, send messages, watch the agent work, and read what it produced. ... A thread is a durable agent conversation on Capy's servers, with a VM attached for execution.
own_agent_api.note: First-party REST API drives Capy's own coding task-agent (Captain/Build): create threads with a prompt, send/interrupt messages, list/read the task tree and transcript. It only drives Capy's own agent, not an arbitrary third-party harness.

mcp_server.quote: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers give Capy access to tools provided by external services and local processes. Once a server is connected, the capy agent (threads and their tasks) can discover and use its tools while working.
mcp_server.note: Capy is an MCP *client* that consumes external MCP servers as tools for its agent; it does not ship its own MCP server for controlling Capy sandboxes.

public_ipv4.quote: Ask Capy to expose a port and it serves that TCP port at a public URL: the way to open a dev server the agent started.
public_ipv4.note: Port access is via a Capy-managed public HTTPS URL/proxy, not a raw public IPv4 address assigned to the machine.

egress_http_rules.quote: A destination can be a hosts alias, a Tailscale IP or CIDR, or another tag ... accept traffic to its port
egress_http_rules.note: The only documented egress control (Tailscale ACLs) is host/port-level for the private tailnet, not HTTP method/path-level rules for general egress.

static_egress_ip.quote: Teams using Capy often ask us if we have static outbound IPs they can allow-list ... Since every Capy thread runs in its own isolated sandbox machine with dynamic addresses, it's hard for us to provide a static list of IP addresses.
static_egress_ip.note: Explicitly stated: no static outbound IP is available.

gpu.quote: Sizes run from Small (1 vCPU, 4 GB) through Big Guy (16 vCPU, 128 GB); the hourly rate for each lives in models & pricing.
gpu.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — machine sizes are CPU/RAM-only coding-agent VMs; no GPU size or GPU add-on is documented.

windows.quote: Every machine is an isolated Ubuntu 24.04 VM where the agent has full control.
windows.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — machines are Ubuntu Linux only.

macos.quote: Every machine is an isolated Ubuntu 24.04 VM where the agent has full control.
macos.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — machines are Ubuntu Linux only.

arm64.quote: Every machine is an isolated Ubuntu 24.04 VM where the agent has full control.
arm64.note: No ARM option is documented anywhere in machine sizing or docs; standard cloud-VM coding-agent infra of this kind is x86-only unless otherwise stated.

self_host.quote: Unlimited parallel agents, SSO, custom environments, and dedicated support. Everything your team needs to ship at scale.
self_host.note: Capy is a hosted service (machines on Latitude.sh, other services on AWS, per the subprocessors page); no documented way to self-host the platform, even on Enterprise. Threads can run on your own computer through the desktop app ('Run threads on your own computer, then move them to the cloud and back', docs.capy.ai/welcome), but the hosted service still runs the agent.

byoc.quote: CUSTOM ENVIRONMENTS: Configure vCPU, RAM, and installed packages per workspace. Run agents in environments that match your production setup.
byoc.note: 'Custom environments' means configuring machine size/packages within Capy's own hosted infrastructure, not deploying Capy into the customer's own cloud account (BYOC); no BYOC option is documented.

open_source.note: Capy runs an 'Open Source Program' that gives free usage credits to qualifying OSS projects; the Capy product itself is closed-source SaaS with no OSI-license release documented.

hipaa.quote: SOC 2 Type II: Independently audited controls for security, availability, and confidentiality.
hipaa.note: Security and enterprise pages list SOC 2 Type II, encryption, SSO, and BYOK as compliance/enterprise features but never mention HIPAA eligibility or a BAA.

eu_data_residency.quote: Latitude.sh | Bare-metal hosting and object storage for agent cloud machines | United States
eu_data_residency.note: Agent machines run in the United States (Latitude.sh). AWS lists 'United States and other AWS regions as configured'. No customer-selectable EU region is documented on the security, enterprise or subprocessors pages.

max_session_h.quote: While the agent works, the machine stays awake automatically. ... There is no stop button; an idle machine sleeps on its own within minutes.
max_session_h.note: No documented hard cap on continuous active-session length; a machine only sleeps after ~2 minutes of the agent being idle, and can be repeatedly kept alive by ongoing agent work or +5 minute extensions, so there is no stated maximum session duration while work continues.

custom_image.quote: Every machine is an isolated Ubuntu 24.04 VM where the agent has full control: it edits files, runs commands, installs packages, and commits code, all without touching your computer.
custom_image.note: Machines are fixed at Ubuntu 24.04; there is no user-supplied base image / Dockerfile-for-the-VM option. Customization is only via per-project setup scripts (initialize/refresh/startup entries, docs.capy.ai/environment) baked into an optional snapshot for fast boot, not a bring-your-own-image mechanism.

ingress_rules.quote: Ask Capy to expose a port and it serves that TCP port at a public URL: the way to open a dev server the agent started. ... The URL works only while the machine is awake.
ingress_rules.note: Exposing a port only creates a plain public URL at Capy's proxy; the docs describe no IP allowlist, auth gate, or security-group-style control over who can reach that URL (only which ports are reserved: 8000/8080/8100/22222). No ingress access-control feature is documented.

egress_allowlist.quote: Capy machines have exactly the access your ACL grants their tag, and nothing else by default. ... "acls": [ { "action": "accept", "src": ["tag:capy"], "dst": ["internal-db:5432"] } ]
egress_allowlist.note: Opt-in Tailscale integration: once a project is enabled, machines join the org's tailnet and can reach only the hosts/ports the org's Tailscale ACLs explicitly grant to the machine's tag (a security-group-style allow list). This governs private tailnet destinations only, not a general internet allow/deny/no-internet mode — ordinary public-internet egress from Docker/the VM remains unrestricted per the machines page ('Containers can pull images and reach the public internet').

usage_api.quote: Read your organization's windowed spend and token totals
usage_api.note: granularity: account-only; cost: yes; The /api/v1/usage endpoint reports organization-level spend and token usage; granularity is account-only, not per-sandbox or per-project.
